negative.answer: No `d.drawImage` — `Draw` cannot rasterize a picture. A picture is an `Image` view (`stretches = cover|contain` for fit, `tint` to recolor), and since the compositing arc it rotates and scales like any view (`rotation`, `scale`, about `pivotX`/`pivotY`) — so a rotated photograph no longer needs a drawing at all. What remains unreachable is compositing a decoded bitmap INSIDE a `draw(d: Draw)` recording.

No app-facing bitmap cache or preload call. Today each `Image` instance decodes its `source` itself — a photograph shown on one surface is decoded again on the next. A platform-managed bitmap store (decode table shared across instances + cached draw rasterizations) is planned — see docs/system-design/ (adaptive draw cache) and the 2026-08-06 assessment; until it lands, the idiom is to keep the SAME view alive across surfaces (one sprung scalar, many followers) rather than to rebuild it.

No hooks, no stores, no props plumbing — state is an attribute declared where it lives (`count: number = 0` on a view), derived state is a `{ }` constraint reading it, and "effects" are the constraint graph's own propagation. A descendant reads an ancestor's attribute by name (`app.count`, `parent.width`, `classroot.…`) — no context, no lifting. Handlers write; constraints react.

No `key=` and no refs — a named member IS its handle (`box: View [ … ]` → `app.box`), and replicated rows take their identity from the record's own `id` field automatically. Reach any node by its dotted path; give records an `id` when their identity matters across reloads.

No SVG element — a vector mark is a `draw(d: Draw)` member (paths, arcs, gradients — a recorded, reactive drawing), the house icons are `Icon` subclasses drawn exactly that way, and an actual `<svg>` you already have lives inside a `DOMIsland`.

No text truncation — there is no ellipsis today. `wrap = false` keeps a run to one line and `clip = true` crops it at the box; slicing the string yourself in a `{ }` constraint is the current idiom for a measured cut. A real `truncate` is a known gap — worth reporting if it blocks you.

No grid layout strategy — `WrappingLayout` flows and wraps; a fixed N-column grid is a small `Layout` subclass of your own (`place()` is ~15 lines of arithmetic over `this.laid()` and `this.view.width`); and tabular DATA wants `Table` or `DataGrid`, which are components, not layouts.

No ZStack and no overlay wrapper — children stack by default: a view with no `layout` imposes no arrangement, and declaration order is z-order (later siblings paint above). Place the layers with x/y; `ignoreLayout = true` floats one child above an arranged set.

No dedicated component — the library is deliberately small, and these are compositions: a card is a `View` (`cornerRadius`, `shadow`, `fill`); a toast is an `ignoreScroll` View a `Spring` slides in; a drawer is a panel whose `x` follows one sprung scalar; a badge is a small rounded `Text` riding its parent's corner; an avatar is an `Image` with `stretches = cover` and rounding. Compose it, then keep it as your own class.

No `requestAnimationFrame` — and though `setTimeout`/`setInterval` exist for host chores, they are never the motion system. Motion is declared: a `Spring` drives an attribute toward a live target (interruptible for free), an `Animator` is the clock-shaped sibling, and per-frame integration (physics you step yourself) is `Heartbeat [ onFrame(dt) ]`, which rides the one shared frame clock. A setTimeout-driven animation fights the settle loop and cannot be interrupted mid-flight; see the guide's Motion & states chapter.

forms.answer:
`class Name extends Base [ … ]` — the one way to define a component. Everything inside the brackets is a MEMBER: `name = value` sets an inherited attribute, `name: Type = value` declares a new one, `name: Type [ … ]` is a named child, `name(args) { … }` a method, `onThing() { … }` an event handler.
A class is not a file and not a module — it is a top-level declaration, and a program is one tree of them (declare.md §4). `extends` may name a class declared LATER in the file. Guide: 04-tree, 11-make-your-own.

`class Name extends Base [ … ]` — single inheritance from another component (a library class or one of your own). The subclass sees every attribute, child, method and event of the base; re-stating an attribute overrides its default, and re-stating a named child extends that child rather than replacing it.
Not top-level in its own right — it is part of a `class` declaration (parser.ts:673). Omit it and you extend `View`. Guide: 11-make-your-own.

`script { … }` — a top-level block of plain TypeScript: constants, functions, model types. Its top-level names are visible from every `{ }` body in the same file, and a constraint may call one — the compiler reads THROUGH the call to find what the body depends on, so a helper does not break reactivity (declare.md §5).
This is where arithmetic and formatting live, so the tree stays about the tree. Guide: 03-relationships, 04-tree.

`include [ "path.declare" ]` — merges another file's TOP-LEVEL DECLARATIONS (its classes, scripts, fonts, styles) into this program, once, however many times it is named. It does not import a root instance and it is not a module system: there are no exports and no namespacing — everything merges into one program.
The path resolves relative to the including file. On a static host the browser compiles the app itself and its include host reads a SYNCHRONOUS map, so app-relative includes must be prefetched (test/static-host.test.mjs pins this). Guide: 04-tree.

`use [ Name, Other ]` — keeps components the build would otherwise DROP. The production build tree-shakes anything no tag instantiates; if your code constructs one by name at runtime (`app.createView("Badge")`), nothing in the tree mentions it and it is removed. `use` is how you say it is still needed (declare.md §4, §7).
The symptom without it is a component that works in dev and is missing from the built app.

`font Name [ … ]` — declares a font family. `Face` children carry the web-font files (weight/style per face); a use site picks the family by name: `fontFamily = [Name, "system-ui"]`, which is a fallback LIST, not a single name.
Declaring a font does not load it — a face loads when something asks for it. Guide: 05-space, 06-style.

`style Name [ … ]` — a named bundle of attribute values a view can wear, so a look is declared once and applied by name rather than copied. Top-level, like `class` (parser.ts's `atTop`).
Distinct from `stylesheet`, which carries THEME TOKENS rather than a bundle of attributes. Guide: 06-style.

`stylesheet Name [ … ]` — declares a swappable SKIN: a dictionary keyed by CLASS name (no selectors, no structural matching, no specificity), resolved by a class-chain walk with field-wise merge, schema-checked at compile time so a stale skin fails loudly. It may carry its own `theme` record, which is what makes a skin theme-aware.
The TOP-LEVEL FORM declares; the View ATTRIBUTE of the same name applies — `stylesheet Dark [ … ]` then `App [ stylesheet = Dark ]`. Same word on purpose: it says what kind of thing `Dark` is, and the syntax already tells them apart.
A sheet is the EXTERNAL channel — style without source edits, imposed on views that never mention it, landing below anything a view sets itself. Compare `styles` (opted into by the view, static after construction) and `theme` (tokens an ancestor provides and bindings read). Guide: 06-style.

`name <- source` — SUBSCRIBE: this member follows a stream or external source, taking each value as it arrives. The tokenizer's `subfrom` (parser.ts). Distinct from `=` (a one-time value) and from `{ }` (a standing relationship over reactive state).
Use it where the value is PUSHED to you from outside the program's own state.

`name <-> :path` — TWO-WAY binding between a leaf input and a data path: edits in the field write back through the cursor (declare.md §9, the leaf-input exception). The tokenizer's `bindtwo` (parser.ts).
Deliberately narrow — it is for editable leaves, not a general mechanism; ordinary bindings are one-way `{ }` so data flow stays traceable.

`method(arg: Type) -> Type { … }` — the RETURN-TYPE marker in a method signature (declare.md §4; the tokenizer's `arrow`). Omit it for a method that returns nothing.
Not a lambda arrow and not a binding operator — inside a `{ }` body or a `script` block, `=>` is ordinary TypeScript.

The four SCOPE NOUNS (declare.md §11) — the only names that reach a node from inside a `{ }` body:
  this       — the member's own node
  parent     — its parent in the tree
  classroot  — the root of the class being defined (how a child reads its class's attributes)
  app        — the program root
They are reserved: a child, method or declared attribute may not take one of these names. `app` compiles to `this.root`, which is why a member named `root` shadows every `app.…` in the same class.

The VALUE CONSTRUCTORS — `gradient(…)`, `stroke(…)`, `shadow(…)`, `stop(…)`, `frost(…)` — build the composite values attributes take: `fill = { gradient("180deg", a, b) }`, `backdrop = { frost(26, 1.5) }`.
Reserved names: none may be used as a member name. Watch the alpha convention — `colorWithAlpha(rgb, a)` takes a 0…255 alpha, not 0…1.

`root` and `children` are STRUCTURAL members the scaffold declares on every View — not scope nouns, not schema attributes, but not free either:
  root      — the node reference `app` compiles to (`app` is `this.root`)
  children  — the node's own child list
A child, method or declared attribute of either name is refused at typecheck. `root` is the sharp one: shadowing it makes every `{ app.… }` in the SAME class resolve against the shadow, and the error surfaces at some unrelated binding.

The SETTLE is the unit in which anything happens at all: a handler's writes are applied together when it returns — constraints re-derive, views appear and retire where data now says so, layout places, sizes update — one indivisible step, run to completion. Nothing paints in the middle of one, and no time passes inside one; motion is many small settles (one per frame), never one long one. (An Animator standing at its destination reads `atRest` — a different fact, on a different clock.)
To finish after your own change has taken effect — aim a camera at a view your write just created — register one step at this settle's close: `afterSettle(app.step)`. Constraint first, afterSettle second, never for waiting. Boot's close is delivered instead: `onReady()`, on the App only.
